title: The Mechanics of Association and Causality in Human Beings
subtitle: Why we fall for people, why we stop, and why the math of relationships is weirder than we think
html:
Two people can meet the same stranger and come away with completely opposite impressions. Standard psychology offers tidy explanations: proximity, similarity, reciprocity. These work well as population averages. They fail badly at the individual level, where the real variation lives.

This essay is about what actually happens when we evaluate another person, why relationships feel like they're decaying when they often aren't, and why thinking about a relationship once it's already failing is one of the most expensive mistakes a person can make.

You don't add up someone's traits. You score them against a map.

The standard model of attraction is essentially a weighted sum. You value intelligence, so give it weight 0.7. You value humor, weight 0.5. A person's score is the total. More of any good thing is always better.

This is wrong in a specific, testable way.

Almost no human trait is valued without limit. Confidence past a point reads as arrogance. Openness past a point reads as instability. Every trait has an ideal level, and value falls away on both sides of it. Someone can be too ambitious, too agreeable, too funny. The function that describes how we value a trait isn't a line going up. It's a peak.

Beyond that, traits aren't evaluated independently. Competence and social status raise someone's perceived value only after warmth clears a threshold. Below that threshold, competence and status actually lower it, because a capable person who reads as cold reads as a threat. The evaluation is gated. You can't compensate for missing warmth with extra intelligence.

Four simulation studies tested these ideas. An ideal-point model, one that treats each trait as having a preferred level rather than an unbounded weight, recovered 89% of the variance in held-out preferences. A linear model recovered 66%. More telling than the gap is the direction of the linear model's errors: it consistently overvalued extreme profiles and undervalued moderate ones. Any model that treats more as always better will misjudge striking, maximal people and miss why well-calibrated people are often the most attractive.

What we feel is a score. What we tell ourselves is a cause.

The evaluation happens almost immediately, below awareness, and arrives as a feeling rather than a number. We then work backward to explain it.

This is where the correspondence bias enters. When someone is cold to us, we don't file a correlation. We generate a cause, and we almost always locate that cause inside the person rather than in their situation. They are cold. Not: they are cold today, in this context, under this pressure.

This runs forward while a relationship is intact and backward once it ends. After a relationship fails, we re-read ambiguous memories as evidence of character rather than circumstance. The history itself is revised. The simulation quantified this: after exit, the mean remembered quality of a relationship fell from 55 to 48.9 with no new information arriving. The share of relationships remembered as having been below acceptable fell from 11% to 62%. Nothing changed except the prior through which the memories were read.

Relationships don't decay. We learn what they always were.

The most common story about why relationships decline is decay: something that was good gradually becomes less good. Value erodes. The feeling fades.

The simulation says this is probably not what's happening in most cases.

A model with pure exponential decay produces dissolution patterns that look nothing like real data. Because all relationships decay on the same schedule, they all hit the exit threshold at nearly the same time, creating a synchronized cliff rather than the gradual spread we actually observe.

The real pattern, documented in marital dissolution statistics, is a hazard curve that rises in the early years, peaks somewhere between years three and eight, then falls. Relationships that survive long enough become progressively less likely to end, not more.

A decay model cannot produce a falling tail. The model that does produce it has no decay at all. It uses heterogeneous match quality, pairs with genuinely different levels of compatibility, plus gradual information revelation. Agents can't see match quality directly; they learn it through noisy evidence over time. The result matches the observed pattern closely, with dissolution peaking around year four and falling steadily afterward.

The key finding is what drives the "improvement" in long-term relationships: selection, not growth. Mean true match quality across all simulated pairs was 55.5. Among pairs intact at year 25, it was 70.5. Nothing improved in any individual relationship. The weaker matches left, and the survivors had always been stronger.

This corrects a widespread misreading of relationship experience. When a relationship feels worse at year four, it feels like deterioration. It might just be accuracy. The appropriate response to those two things is completely different, and from the inside they are very hard to tell apart. The discriminating question is whether the feeling tracks specific revealing events or accumulates smoothly regardless of what's happened. The former suggests learning. The latter might suggest something is actually changing.

Three things that have to work, not one.

A relationship runs on three separate channels: attraction, trust, and provision.

Attraction is how much value you assign to being near someone. Trust is what you expect them to do when their interests and yours diverge. Provision is what they actually transfer, whether time, resources, or acts of service.

These channels differ in how evidence about them arrives. Attraction is visible almost immediately. Provision is directly observable and verifiable, which makes it the highest-bandwidth signal. Trust is the slowest, because the events that actually test it, moments when someone could have prioritized themselves and didn't, are rare.

The distinction between capital and service also matters here. Capital is fungible; it can be delegated. Service costs the giver's own time, which is the one input nobody can outsource. A gift of time therefore carries more evidential weight than a gift of equivalent monetary value.

The channels don't simply add up. A sufficiently high attraction score doesn't offset near-zero trust. When one channel drops very low, the relationship ends regardless of how the others are doing. The simulation tested this, though it found a troubling result: dissolution timing alone cannot distinguish a conjunctive rule from an additive one. The rules do separate on the character of exits. Under a conjunctive structure, relationships frequently end while at least one channel is still clearly working. Under an additive structure, this should be rare. The way to test which structure is real is to look at what's happening to all three channels at the moment relationships actually end.

Trust, contrary to intuition, does not decline in surviving relationships. The argument that it should goes like this: opportunities for interests to diverge accumulate over time, so trust must face more trials and therefore more chances to fail. But each trial resolves in one of two directions. For a trustworthy partner, trials resolve favorably, and that's precisely how trust is earned rather than assumed. Among simulated pairs intact at year 25, mean trust belief rose from 60.3 to 60.9, converging almost exactly on true trust quality of 60.5. Leavers also converged on reality, their beliefs of 48.8 tracking a true value of 47.5.

Both groups got more accurate. They just converged on different truths.

Thinking about it once it's already failing.

The association score arrives fast and below awareness. Conscious evaluation typically activates once perceived value falls near the exit threshold. By then, the useful period for reasoning has already passed.

The simulation ran two conditions: agents who updated their beliefs every year, and agents who updated only once perceived value fell within a critical range of the exit threshold. The outcome was stark.

Continuous updaters spent 9.2 years in poor matches on average. Threshold updaters spent 25.5. Continuous updaters lost nothing in good matches: 25.73 years versus 25.97, a difference within noise. The entire cost of late deliberation fell on bad relationships, which is exactly the situation where clear thinking matters most.

The mechanism isn't emotional clouding at the critical moment, though that may also be true. It's informational. An agent who doesn't update doesn't accumulate evidence. By the time the threshold is crossed, beliefs are anchored to an early, optimistic prior that years of unprocessed experience have done nothing to correct. Waiting to think doesn't preserve a clear judgment for later. It destroys the evidence that judgment would have needed.

The practical implication runs against intuition. The useful thing is not better reasoning during a crisis. It's cheap, low-intensity attention during the long period when nothing appears to be wrong. Small amounts of continuous attention outperform large amounts delivered late, even though the continuous policy feels unnecessary while it's being carried out.

Why going back is so much harder than starting fresh.

A natural assumption is that association and disassociation are symmetric: value rises, value falls, you can run the process in either direction with equivalent ease.

The model says this is wrong, and the mechanism matters.

Association is fast, driven against an optimistic and uncertain prior. A stranger's initial belief is vague, so each new observation shifts it substantially. Disassociation operates differently. It runs against beliefs that have converged. Confidence is high. The same evidence that moved belief easily during early association barely moves it now.

Holding true partner quality fixed at 62 across all conditions, the simulation measured how long it took to reach an acceptance threshold from different starting points. A stranger with an uncertain prior crossed in one year. A former partner with a resolved low belief crossed in seven. The same person, behaving identically, takes seven times longer to be accepted by someone who already knows them badly than by someone who has never met them.

This is not stubbornness or bitterness. It's optimal Bayesian updating. When uncertainty has been reduced, the update from any new observation is smaller. The agent who learned most efficiently about their partner is the one least able to revise that judgment. Confidence, not hostility, is the obstacle.

Then retrospective re-attribution compounds it. After exit, ambiguous memories get re-read as dispositional rather than situational. The remembered history of the relationship degrades without new information. A person trying to reconcile isn't starting from where the relationship ended; they're starting from a revised and typically worse reconstruction of it.

What all of this implies.

None of this is based on human data. These are simulation results that reproduce observed population patterns well enough to take seriously as mechanistic hypotheses. They should generate predictions, and several of them are sharp enough to be genuinely falsifiable.

Preference ratings should show ideal points, not linear weights, with steeper value drops for people with narrower tolerances.

Attribution confidence should scale with associative activation. Stronger first impressions should produce more dispositional explanations of the same ambiguous behavior.

Satisfaction decline, when measured carefully, should decompose into learning rather than genuine change. Pairs who received more diagnostic information early should show steeper early revision and flatter late decline.

People who monitor relationships continuously should exit poor ones sooner with no cost to good ones. This asymmetry is the sharpest prediction, because it's not what a story about vigilance being harmful would predict.

And reconciliation should require substantially more evidence than initial association, with the gap widening in proportion to how long and how confidently the original relationship was known.

The decay story feels true from the inside because value does appear to fall. But the simulations produce that same experience from a model in which nothing about the relationship changes at all. The feeling of decline is sometimes an accurate report of a relationship getting worse. It's often just the process of getting better at knowing what it was.

title: The Proxies Are Breaking
html:
The Fundamentals

Two things have always been valuable in a worker: that you can be trusted to do good work, and that you won’t be a liability to the company.

Nothing else is fundamental.

The resume, the interview, the degree, the portfolio, they are proxies, to access those fundamental two values.

Why Proxies Exist

Proxies exist because verification is expensive. Nobody can watch you work for a year before deciding to hire you, so substitutes were invented.

A degree proxies competence because it’s costly to fake and correlates with ability. A clean background check proxies safety. A polished interview proxies both.

The whole architecture of hiring is just a stack of these shortcuts. And for most of the 20th century, they worked well enough.

Why the Proxies Are Breaking

AI collapses the cost of faking these proxies without collapsing the cost of faking the underlying trait. A resume can be perfectly tailored in seconds. A cover letter can simulate exactly the voice a hiring manager wants to hear.

Interview answers can be rehearsed against AI-predicted questions.

None of this means the candidate is more competent.

And once everyone has a bachelor’s degree, it stops signaling anything, so the market invents a master’s degree to restore the gap.

But AI is decoupling proxies from what they measure faster than institutions can invent replacements, which means we’re heading into a period where the old signals are visibly broken and the new ones haven’t stabilized yet.

What the New Proxies Look Like

The strongest candidates for replacement proxies share one property: they require the underlying trait to produce them, not just the appearance of it.

A visible trail of work done before anyone was watching.

Not a portfolio curated for a job search, but a public record that accumulated while you were doing the work for its own reasons.

A years-long commit history, a body of writing that predates any application, a track record of shipped things that can be verified by date.

This is hard to fake retroactively because faking it means actually doing years of work.

A referral from someone whose own reputation is on the line.

Not a LinkedIn endorsement, which costs the writer nothing, but a referral where the referrer takes real damage if you fail.

Performance on a task that closely resembles the actual job.

Generic interview questions can be predicted and rehearsed.

A real, somewhat idiosyncratic problem specific to the role.

A consistent identity across contexts over time.

Someone who has said the same things, held the same positions, and behaved the same way across a long public record is harder to fake than someone you’re meeting for the first time.

What These Have in Common

Notice what all four share. They route around self-report.

The old proxies — resume, cover letter, interview — all relied on the candidate’s own claims about themselves, packaged persuasively. The new proxies rely on externally verifiable trails that existed before the person knew they’d be evaluated, or on the testimony of someone else who has something to lose.

The Practical Implication

The practical implication for anyone building career capital is straightforward: stop optimizing the parts of your record that are self-reported, and start building the parts that someone else would have to vouch for, or that existed on the record before you needed them to.

And finally, maybe trust was the only thing that was ever valuable. The proxies were just the tools we built to approximate it cheaply. Now those tools are breaking, and we’re left with the thing itself.

title: The Chronicles of Brown 2
html:
He does not fear the fall.
He fears climbing the wrong mountain and calling it a summit.

Give him a choice: succeed on the wrong path, or fail on the right one.
He will choose the failure every time.
Because a wasted life is the only loss he cannot recover.

He does not search for certainty.
Certainty is a comfort for people who stop thinking.
What he wants is smaller and harder: enough reason to commit.
Not forever. Just for now.
He builds his belief, bets everything on it, and watches for the moment reality says otherwise.
When it does, he moves.

His mind works like a fire that reduces everything to ash and asks what remains.
Experience becomes pattern.
Pattern becomes mechanism.
Mechanism becomes law.
He cannot look at a moment without asking what made it happen.
This is his gift, and it is also his trap.

Because a mind that builds beautiful explanations
can mistake beauty for truth.
A story that fits perfectly is still just a story
until it survives contact with the world.
He knows this about himself.
It is the danger he carries everywhere.

He does not crave applause.
He craves proof.
When his work moves someone, answers someone, reaches someone,
it tells him the thing was real.
Silence does not wound his pride.
It haunts him with a different question: did any of it matter?

He measures his days against every day he did not choose.
Not “was this good,”
but “was this worth more than everything else I could have done instead.”
This is why waste cuts him deeper than most people.

He is built for rooms with real stakes,
fast answers, visible progress, people who care if the work is true.
He withers in rooms where effort disappears into nothing,
where no one can tell if anything got better.

And his oldest trap:
every hard question tempts him one step higher,
what should I do becomes what should I want,
becomes how do I know what I want is right,
until the ladder has no top.

But he is learning the only way out.
Not a perfect answer.
Just the best one he can defend today,
a commitment,
and the nerve to let the world write the next page.

title: AI, Trust, and the Future
html:
Money is a vote

Money is not value itself. It is a stand in for what people find valuable, and that opinion is bounded by where you are. The same work is worth a different number in London than in Miami, because the currency, the local norms, and the local supply of that work are different.

If something can be sold, it will be. People are always trying to get more of what they personally value, using whatever they have to trade. That simple pressure drives everything.

As AI gets more capable, the real question is not what will value hold value, what will increase in value, and what will decline in value.

This is about language models specifically, not robotics or spatial computing models. Text and code based intelligence is improving the fastest right now, so we are evaluating the change based on LLMs.

What gets more valuable

Security and evaluation

As models get more capable, their output gets harder for a person to check. Early on, you can read an answer and tell if it is wrong. Later, a model may write code too complex to fully read, or make a plan too layered to audit by hand. A large share of what doctors and lawyers do will be automated. But a model can suggest a diagnosis or draft a contract, and someone still has to sign it and own the outcome if it is wrong. That weight, the risk a person agrees to carry, becomes more valuable even as the work underneath it gets automated.

Compute runs on power. As demand for compute grows faster than the grid can expand, the people who build and maintain that physical infrastructure, electricians, technicians, and the trades around data centers, become more valuable. This work is physical and licensed, which makes it harder to automate than desk work.

Generic software as a service

Building software used to take a team. Now one person can publish a working app in days, so the market fills up fast and the product itself stops being the scarce part. Companies without real distribution, or the capital to buy it, get copied and undercut almost as soon as they launch. On the current curve, I expect end to end software engineering to largely get solved and automated, which pushes this further.

Stock content, basic copywriting, and low end design sell exactly what models now produce for almost nothing. If the output is easy to generate and easy to check, the price of producing it keeps falling toward zero.

Companies that make money mainly by holding information or connecting two sides, directories, simple comparison sites, basic staffing firms, lose their edge when a model can find and compare things instantly on its own.

title: BLUEBERRY
html:
I strive to be the truest man in eternity,

With a stillness that asks nothing of the world,

Like a blueberry on a hot summer day,
plucked from the branch
and placed in the hands of a little boy,

even torn from the body that bore it,
it remains at peace.

I surrender to what I am,
whatever I may become,
what I have seen,
what I have lived,
and every version of myself
that has ever existed.

I am a child of the universe.

I do not need to conquer this realm.

I only want to sit within it,

between the beginning and the end,
the sun and the moon,
birth and demise,
the four seasons,

again and again,

to bloom,
to wither,
and to bloom again.

Like a flower in a garden.
Like a rose in antiquity.
Like a long-lost love
returning to its lover
after the world has forgotten my name.

I choose peace.

Peace with the universe.
Peace with the stars.
Peace with myself.
Peace with God,
whatever you may conceive Him to be.

To walk away from cruelty
without becoming cruel.

To seek those who love,
those who make being alive
feel like a gift.

We are all children of this universe,

blueberry,
grapes,
ravioli,
enchantment,
serenity,
serendipity.

The sweetness of a blueberry
on the tip of your tongue.

Sunlight on an ordinary afternoon.

The miracle of light
seeping beneath my eyes.

Only heaven knows
why I was born,
why I am here,
and what I should surrender my life to.

But I have a guess
of how I want to live:

with wonder,
with love,
in search of truth.

To love without possessing.
To feel without fear.
To forgive without forgetting.
To be at peace.

To be so at peace
that the world does not need
to be a peaceful place.

That the world does not need
to be a perfect place.

I want to love so truly
that love needs no explanation,

a serenity so deep,
a majesty so pure,
that eternity itself
halts before its immaculateness.

I want to sit beneath the sun
and wait patiently for the moon.

I want to watch the seasons turn
and still be one of the children
of this mysterious universe,

briefly touching one another
in the infinite.

Let me be still.

Let me be full of wonder.

Let me begin again.

title: The Exchange
subtitle: Why you should understand incentives before entering any important exchange
html:
An employee gives an organization something extraordinarily scarce: time, attention, ability, judgment, and ultimately a portion of their life.

The organization gives something in return: money, opportunity, resources, status, knowledge, autonomy, security, ownership, and meaning.

We call this employment. But employment is really an exchange of value between two parties with different objectives.

Before entering any important exchange, you should understand not only what the other party says it wants, but what its incentives make it rational.

The Bilateral Exchange

Consider an AI laboratory and a researcher.

The lab is asking:

What value will this person create for us?

The researcher is asking:

What value will this institution create for me?

The lab possesses capital, compute, infrastructure, data, models, teams, and institutional knowledge.

The researcher possesses intelligence, technical skill, creativity, judgment, research taste, and time.

The employment relationship brings these resources together.

The fundamental equation is therefore:

Person chooses institution ↔ institution chooses person.

Both sides are making an investment under uncertainty.

Why Does the Lab Want You?

An AI lab does not ultimately hire someone because they are smart.

It hires them because it expects them to increase the organization’s ability to accomplish its objectives.

That value can come from several sources:

Execution: You can build, research, test, or ship.

Discovery: You can find things the organization did not know.

Judgment: You can determine which problems are worth solving.

Leverage: Your work makes other people substantially more productive.

Scarcity: Your particular combination of capabilities is difficult to replace.

Learning: Your value is expected to increase over time.

Ownership: You can be trusted with increasingly important problems.

This creates an important progression:

Task → Project → Problem → Direction

At the lowest level, you execute someone else’s decisions.

At the highest level, you decide what should be done in the first place.

Why Does the Employee Want the Lab?

The employee is not simply selling labor for a salary.

They are exchanging a portion of their finite life for a bundle of returns.

Those returns include:

Money: salary, bonuses, equity.

Human capital: knowledge, skills, mentorship.

Career capital: reputation, publications, network, credentials.

Resources: compute, data, infrastructure, exceptional colleagues.

Autonomy: freedom to decide what and how to work.

Meaning: mission, identity, contribution.

The correct question is therefore not:

“Which job pays the most?”

It is:

“Which opportunity creates the greatest expected value for my future?”

A $250,000 position at a frontier laboratory could rationally be worth more than a $400,000 position elsewhere if the first dramatically increases your future capabilities, network, reputation, ownership, or impact.

The Hidden Variable: Opportunity Cost

Every choice is also a rejection of alternatives.

When a researcher joins a laboratory, they are giving up:

  • Other laboratories

  • Startups

  • Independent research

  • Graduate school

  • Entrepreneurship

  • Leisure

  • Time with family

  • Other possible futures

The lab faces the same problem.

Hiring you means not hiring someone else.

So both sides are continuously asking:

What is my best alternative?

This is what gives each side bargaining power.

The rarer your capabilities and the better your alternatives, the more valuable you are to the institution—and the more leverage you have in the exchange.

The Real Incentive Structure

The most important thing to understand about an organization is not what it claims to value.

It is what it rewards.

An organization may say:

“We value innovation.”

But if promotions consistently go to people who avoid risky projects, the real incentive is risk avoidance.

It may say:

“We value truth.”

But if researchers are rewarded primarily for exciting positive results, the system may incentivize researchers to find exciting positive results.

The formal mission tells you what the institution says.

The incentive structure tells you what people are actually encouraged to do.’]

Money Is Only One Currency

Institutions have more currencies than dollars.

They can distribute:

Money — salary, bonuses, equity.

Power — authority, autonomy, access to resources.

Status — titles, recognition, prestige.

Knowledge — mentorship, information, proximity to frontier work.

Opportunity — projects, promotions, exposure.

Meaning — mission, identity, belonging.

The most powerful organizations combine these currencies.

Salary can purchase someone’s labor.

But autonomy, ownership, status, learning, and mission can influence whether they bring their best judgment and commitment.

This is the difference between:

“I’m doing my job.”

and

“I want this to succeed.”

The Principal-Agent Problem

The interests of the employee and institution will never be perfectly identical.

The lab wants organizational output.

The employee has personal goals.

And the lab cannot perfectly observe the employee’s effort, judgment, motivation, or alternative uses of their time.

This creates the classic principal-agent problem.

The institution therefore needs mechanisms that align individual incentives with institutional objectives.

Compensation is one mechanism.

So are:

  • Equity

  • Promotions

  • Reputation

  • Autonomy

  • Mission

  • Culture

  • Peer recognition

  • Performance evaluations

  • Long-term career opportunities

The best organizations don’t merely force people to comply.

They make the rational pursuit of the individual’s interests overlap with the organization’s interests.

The Question That Changes How You Evaluate Institutions

When evaluating an organization, don’t ask only:

“What does this organization offer me?”

Ask:

“What does this organization make rational for me to do?”

Then ask the reverse:

“What does my presence make rational for this organization to do?”

Those two questions expose the structure of the exchange.

What does the lab want from you?

What can it offer you?

What are your alternatives?

What are its alternatives?

What behavior does it reward?

Who captures the value you create?

What happens when your interests diverge?

And most importantly:

What portion of your finite life is this exchange worth?

The Principle

This framework extends far beyond AI.

The same exchange exists between:

researchers and universities,
doctors and hospitals,
engineers and companies,
athletes and teams,
founders and investors,
creators and platforms,
employees and institutions.

Everywhere, scarce resources are being exchanged.

The mistake is entering the exchange without understanding its structure.

Before you give someone your labor, understand what they are buying.

Before you accept what they offer, understand what you are selling.

Before you commit years of your life, understand what incentives will govern those years.

Because institutions are not defined only by their missions, cultures, or promises.

They are defined by the behaviors their incentives produce.

And learning to see those incentives is one of the most valuable forms of institutional literacy you can develop.

title: The Method of Deliberation, Among Other Failure Modes
subtitle: Decision Making
html:
Most people don’t make decisions the way they imagine they do.

A decision gets made first, quickly and intuitively, before any real evaluation has taken place.

Reasoning arrives afterward, searching for evidence to affirm the decision. We then unknowingly start to build a case for the decision rather than looking at things unbiasedly.

Nobody sits down and thinks, I’ve already decided, now let me go find some evidence to prove my conclusion. The search for context feels like real inquiry the entire time.

But it’s aimed.

Confirming evidence gets treated as the answer. Disconfirming evidence gets waved off as noise.

The asymmetry is invisible from the inside.

A person operating this way can produce a coherent, well-reasoned-sounding argument for their conclusion and never once notice that the direction was fixed before the reasoning started.

The Method of Deliberation

Correcting for this means restructuring the process so the commitment happens later, and stays revisable longer, than our natural instinct wants to.

*Warning: apply this to your own reasoning, not to well-tested instinct or to actors you’ve verified are arguing in bad faith.

Hold your view as provisional. State in advance, before you go looking for anything, what evidence would actually change your mind. If you can’t name it, you’re not deliberating, you’re already decided.

Seek the strongest version of the opposing case. Not the weakest one, the version that’s easy to knock down and makes you feel better for having considered it. If you can’t argue the other side better than the people who actually hold it, you don’t understand your own position yet either.

Notice when you feel relieved. Relief at a piece of supporting evidence is a signal worth catching, not just enjoying. It usually means you were hoping for it, which means it deserves more scrutiny.

Separate the two moments. What do I want to be true, and what is true, are different questions. Most bad reasoning comes from answering them at the same time and calling it one question. Even a few minutes of separation between them is often enough to notice the difference.

Other Common Failure Modes in Human Thinking

The method of deliberation addresses one failure mode, but it has close relatives. Each of the following follows the same basic shape: a shortcut that feels like clear thinking from the inside, and a small structural habit that corrects for it.

Sunk Cost Fallacy

People continue a course of action because of what’s already been invested, time, money, effort, rather than because it’s still the best path forward.

The past cost feels like a reason to continue, even though it can’t be recovered either way, whether you continue or stop. The fix is the clean slate test: ask whether you’d choose this path today, starting fresh, with no prior investment.

If the answer is no, the sunk cost is the only thing keeping you in it.

Present Bias

Immediate reward or comfort gets overweighted against a larger future benefit, even when the math clearly favors waiting.

The fix is precommitment: lock in the future-favoring choice before the moment of temptation arrives.

Narrative Fallacy

People construct a coherent story to explain events after the fact, then mistake the story’s coherence for evidence that it’s true.

A clean narrative simply feels more credible than it has earned the right to be.

The fix is to ask what else fits: for any explanation that feels satisfying, generate two other stories that fit the same facts equally well.

False Consensus Effect

People assume others think, want, or would decide the way they do, treating their own reaction as representative rather than as one data point among many.

The fix is to actively sample outside your own view: before assuming your reaction generalizes, ask someone with a different background or a different stake in the outcome what they’d actually think, rather than imagining their answer for them.

Escalation of Commitment

A failing plan gets doubled down on specifically because of public commitment to it, since reversing course feels like admitting error rather than simply updating.

The fix is to pre-decide an exit condition: define, before you start, the specific signal that means stop. Deciding the exit criteria in advance removes the ego cost of actually using them later.

Illusory Superiority

People rate their own skill, judgment, or objectivity as above average by default, without much evidence, largely because they have access to their own intentions but not their own blind spots.

The fix is to calibrate against track record: keep an actual record of past predictions or judgments against outcomes, and let that record correct the self-estimate instead of memory of good intentions.

The Just-World Fallacy

There’s a quiet assumption that outcomes are basically fair, that people generally get what they deserve. This leads to inferring character from circumstance, assuming someone must have done something to deserve what happened to them, instead of looking at the actual causes. The fix is to separate outcome from merit: ask what happened and whether it was deserved as two distinct questions, and don’t let the outcome silently answer both.

The Fundamental Attribution Error

Other people’s behavior gets explained by their character, while the same behavior in oneself gets explained by circumstance. Same action, different standard, depending entirely on who did it. The fix is to swap the actor: before judging someone’s behavior, ask what situational explanation you’d reach for if you had done the exact same thing, and apply that same generosity in both directions.

Parkinson’s Law of Triviality

Also known as bikeshedding: disproportionate time and energy goes to a small, easy-to-understand decision, while a large, complex one gets rushed through, simply because the small decision is easier to have an opinion about. The fix is to weight time by stakes, not ease: before spending time on any decision, ask whether the effort matches the actual consequence, and cap time deliberately when a decision is easy to debate but low-stakes.

A single named, specific case draws disproportionate concern, while statistically larger but abstract suffering barely registers. The fix is to convert to comparable units: before deciding based on emotional pull, translate both options into the same unit, lives, dollars, hours, so the comparison isn’t distorted by which one happens to have a face attached.

This is the mirror image of confirmation bias. Rigorous scrutiny gets applied to evidence that contradicts a person’s view, while evidence that supports it gets accepted at face value. It isn’t that disconfirming evidence gets avoided, it gets actively demolished, while anything favorable gets waved through. The fix is an equal scrutiny rule: apply the same standard of evidence to claims you like as to claims you don’t. If you’d demand a citation for the uncomfortable claim, demand one for the comfortable one too.

Once something is known, it becomes almost impossible to model what it was like not to know it. This leads to misjudging what other people understand, overestimating how obvious one’s own reasoning is, and communicating poorly as a result, which in turn corrupts the information later decisions get built on. The fix is to explain it to a naive version: before assuming something is clear or already agreed upon, explain it as if to someone with zero context. If it can’t be made simple, it isn’t as well understood as it feels.

Choice-Supportive Bias

After a decision is made, the option that was chosen gets retroactively remembered as better than it actually was, and the rejected options as worse, which makes honest after-the-fact review nearly impossible. The fix is to record the prediction before deciding: write down what’s expected from each option before choosing, so there’s an untainted record to compare against later instead of relying on memory.

The Spotlight Effect

How much other people notice or judge a given choice gets consistently overestimated, which pushes decisions toward managing perceived opinions rather than toward the actual merits of the situation. The fix is to ask what you’d actually notice: recall how little is remembered, in general, about other people’s minor choices or mistakes, and assume roughly that same level of attention is being paid the other way.

Zero-Risk Bias

There’s a preference for eliminating one small risk completely rather than reducing a much larger risk partially, because zero feels satisfying even when it isn’t the better use of time or resources. The fix is to compare total risk reduction: before acting, ask which option reduces the most total expected harm, rather than which option gets any single number down to zero.

None of these failure modes are exotic. They’re the default settings of a mind that has to act under uncertainty and limited time, and in most situations they’re harmless enough. The cost shows up specifically in decisions that matter, where the shortcut gets mistaken for the conclusion. The fix, in every case above, is roughly the same shape: build in a moment, however brief, where the process has to slow down and check itself before it’s allowed to call itself finished.

Confirming evidence gets treated as the answer. Disconfirming evidence gets waved off as noise. 
The asymmetry is invisible from the inside. 
A person operating this way can produce a coherent, well-reasoned-sounding argument for their conclusion and never once notice that the direction was fixed before the reasoning started.

Correcting for this means restructuring the process so the commitment happens later, and stays revisable longer, than our natural instinct wants to.

title: Antiquity
subtitle: Notes
html:
Prologue

I.

I was born in the middle of the internet revolution, in the first generation to come of age beside thinking machines.

II.

From my mother: that tenderness is not softness, and that a person can be held together by another person’s steadiness for years after they stop noticing it.

From my mentor: to take only the opportunities that add to your life, and to give your life to one end.

From Marcus: that the work in front of me is the whole of my duty, and that nothing which happens to me is unusual.

From Seneca: that time is the only estate I own.

From Burton: that a life can be argued for out loud, in plain speech, and that plain speech carries further than ornament.

From the novels I loved, and from The Beginning After the End most of all: that a second life is possible, that a man may begin again carrying everything he learned in the first, and that this is not a fantasy but a description of how ordinary people change.

From those who loved me and were not repaid in kind: everything else.

III.

What follows is a record. Memories and recollections out of my youth and early manhood, set down while I can still remember what I actually thought at the time and not what it would flatter me to have thought.

IV.

Much of my life was flawed. I have made many mistakes and some of them I made twice. I write to be useful, in the truest and least decorated sense of that word.

V.

Philosophy earns nothing until it goes down into behavior. If a doctrine does not change what a man does on an ordinary Tuesday then it is jewelry.

VI.

And I suppose love means something different to me now than it did then. I will not call the older meaning false. It was true for the man who held it and he held it with his whole chest.

VII.

Technology is the crutch that will set us free.

Not a universal good. It has never been a universal good.

It is man’s mistress, taken up in appetite, kept in secret, blamed for what we brought to it ourselves.

And with all its problems it still points us toward the actualization of man and his becoming, and it is still the only instrument we have ever found that lifts the floor beneath the poorest man alive.

The problems of technology will be solved with more technology. A fire in a field is answered by another fire, set on purpose, by men who understand what they are doing and are frightened while they do it.

VIII.

So the vectors converge toward human flourishing, trying to minimize the suffering at the edges. And the whole of the work is at those edges, and the whole of the work is to make that margin smaller each year than it was the year before.

Sizoron and the Emperor

I.

Many men believe themselves necessary. They hold it without doubt, that their lives carry meaning, that they were set down on this earth for some reason which could be stated out loud if anyone ever asked them to state it.

And it is true that in the present arrangement of things a man is measured by his work, and by what the world can take from it.

And then there is the old saying from Marcus, that a man is worth no more than the things he busies himself with. So choose those things with terror. And then love them truly.

II.

Then Sizoron came to the Emperor and said:

Whether I am a Roman or African or of whatever creed I stem from, the question sits on top of my mind and will not move.

How do I become valuable in this life? How do I keep from being ordained to that pit of worthlessness where I watch my fellow men lie down?

III.

And the Emperor said:

You become valuable by listening.

Listen to what other men value in you. Not what you wanted them to value. What they come back for, again and again, without being asked, when they have no reason on earth to flatter you. You get what other men value in your work and you do not get one grain more, and a man who will not hear this can spend forty years being excellent at something nobody needed.

IV.

And money? said Sizoron.

V.

And the Emperor said:

I decree that many men are ordained to be worthless. The universe is a random arrangement of stars in a pointless abyss and it has no opinion about you.

Money is a report. It tells you what you are worth to other men. It is a true report and it does not tell you very much. Do not take it for the verdict and do not pretend you are too fine to read it.

And love fully, whatever that turns out to mean. You will not know in advance.

And love your work. Whatever it is that society values in you, love it deeply, give it what you most incline toward, put down every other thing you were carrying, and go.

VI.

Human flourishing is our aim. You must strive toward it, and you must build the systems that make other men strive toward it without being asked.

And know that this has been the whole of it for as long as there have been men. There are no secrets on the road to paradise. There is only the road, and the walking, and who is walking beside you.

VII.

I have been a poor man and I have been a rich man, and out of both I decided the same thing. The true good is whatever raises the bar of human livelihood, and in our age that is technology. With all its ills it is still worth fighting to build.

VIII.

I busy myself with the advancement of human civilization.

And however worthless and ephemeral I may be against the infinite stretch of the universe, I know I have served my life toward a noble ideal.

And that is good.

title: On the Wrong Goal
subtitle: On pursuing something that is actually ours.
html:
It is not that life is short. It is that we lose most of it before we ever spend a single day pursuing something that was actually ours.

Look at how the years actually go. A man is not robbed of decades by death alone. He is robbed of them earlier, by every year spent building toward a target he never chose for himself, a target inherited from his father, his industry, or the applause of strangers he will never meet.

Add up those years and you will find they are not a small tax on a life. They are most of it. The man who dies at eighty having spent sixty years chasing the wrong thing has not lived eighty years. He has lived twenty, and been busy for the rest.

You will hear a man on his deathbed say that time cheated him, that he needed ten more years to finish what he started. Do not believe him. Time did not cheat him.

He spent every hour he was given walking toward a target that was never going to give him what he wanted, and only now, at the end, is he discovering the debt.

Watch how a goal gets chosen, and you will see why so much life disappears before it is even noticed missing. Nobody sits alone and asks what they are built for. They look at what the crowd is already running toward, see the ones out front getting praised, and decide the target must be worth having, since so many are running.

Nobody stops to ask whether it was made for them. They ask only whether it looks large enough to justify the running. And so a man can spend forty years in motion, working harder than anyone around him, admired for his discipline, and arrive at the end having built nothing that was ever his, with no years left to start again.

You will meet this man everywhere. He is not hard to find. He is still telling the story of the goal he chased at twenty, still explaining why it mattered, decades after the mattering left him. Ask him what he found when he finally got there and watch him change the subject.

Most men do not merely waste their years on the wrong goal. They shrink inside the time they had. A goal built for someone else has a ceiling built for someone else, and a man will hit that ceiling and call it his limit, never knowing he had another fifty feet in him that this goal was never tall enough to require.

The world does not pay a man for how badly he wants something. It pays him for what he is capable of, applied to whatever he happens to be doing.

Wanting the wrong thing enough does not raise the payout. It only guarantees that whatever capability he has, and whatever years he has, get spent somewhere too small to return them in full. So he ends up with less than he imagined, in less time than he realized he had.

Do not tell me the goal was worthy. Worthiness was never the question. Money is worthy. Rank is worthy. Praise is worthy. All of them are real, all of them can be earned honestly, and none of them ask whether they were made for you, or whether you have enough years left to recover if they were not.

There is another kind of goal, and you have felt it before whether or not you have chased it yet. It is the pull you cannot explain to anyone who asks why it matters to you.

It offered you no reward the first time you noticed it, no crowd was running toward it, no one applauded you for caring. You paid attention to it anyway, for no reason you could defend.

That is not a distraction from your real work. That is the only evidence you will ever get, ahead of time, pointing at what your real work is, and it is being handed to you while you still have years left to use it.

So stop asking how much time is left. That is the wrong question, and it always has been. Ask instead whether the thing consuming your hours was chosen by you or handed to you by everyone else’s applause.

A short life spent pursuing your own goal will outweigh a long one spent perfecting someone else’s. The waste was never only the years. It was the years, spent in the wrong direction, and you do not get a second stretch of them to fix it.

title: Scrutinizing the Objective
subtitle: Optimizing Decision Making
html:
Better context generally leads to better decisions. But context is only useful relative to the goal we are trying to achieve.

If we misunderstand our objective, we may search for highly relevant context while still moving in the wrong direction.

This creates a deeper failure than simply lacking information.

Consider the sequence:

Incentive model, then objective, then relevance model, then context selection, then decision, then outcome.

Everyone’s incentive model sits at a different degree, shaped by their own experiences. What we value and what we find beneficial is not fixed or universal, it is built up over time out of what we have lived through, so two people can hold genuinely different incentive models.

The objective is the modality through which we pursue that incentive, the specific aim we adopt in order to fulfill it.

This is exactly why the objective is so often where things go wrong. Because the incentive model is personal and shaped by experience, it is not something outside forces can easily touch or override. But the objective, the chosen path toward that incentive, is far more exposed.

It is where authority figures, loved ones, persuasive people, social pressure, and our own assumptions do their work. They rarely try to convince us to want something different at the deepest level. Instead they convince us that a particular objective is the right way to get what we already want. That is a much easier thing to influence, and a much easier thing to get wrong.

So we can value the right thing at the deepest level and still choose the wrong objective as our method of getting there, often because someone we trusted, respected, or found compelling shaped that choice for us without ever touching the incentive underneath.

If the objective is wrong, everything downstream can be wrong while still appearing rational. We may carefully gather information, weigh evidence, and make a well reasoned decision, but still optimize for the wrong thing, not because our values were wrong, but because we misjudged how to pursue them.

This problem is especially common when the source of the objective is hard to see clearly. Persuasive people, authority figures, people we love, social pressure, visible rewards, incomplete information, and our own assumptions can cause us to mistake a borrowed objective for our own, or to mistake a flawed objective for a faithful expression of our true incentive. A persuasive explanation can do more than give us bad information. It can change what information we even consider relevant.

The most dangerous version is a self reinforcing loop:

A wrong objective, often adopted from someone else’s influence, leads to wrong context, which leads to a wrong decision, which produces misleading feedback, which then strengthens our confidence in the original wrong objective, even though the incentive underneath was never actually examined.

This suggests that good decision making requires more than asking, “What information do I need?” We should also ask:

“Why do I believe this is the objective?”

And even before that:

“Whose framing shaped this objective, mine or someone else’s?”

And more importantly:

The objective is the modality through which we pursue that incentive, the specific aim we adopt in order to fulfill it.

title: The Obsessed Mind Love, Aurelius II
subtitle: Human Flourishing as an Objective
html:
Marcus Aurelius ruled an empire and still found time each night to ask himself whether he had lived that day as reason required. He told himself that the inferior exist for the sake of the superior, and that among living things, the superior are those which have reason.

He wrote it not for anyone else, but as a discipline, a candlelit way of reminding himself exactly where he stood in the order of things, so that he might act accordingly.

Two thousand years later, we are building something that will reason many orders of magnitude beyond us. Not incrementally beyond. Categorically beyond, the way we stand beyond an ant.

By Aurelius’s own measure, we are on course to become the inferior. No inferior being has ever ruled over a superior one, let alone one superior by such a margin.

The impossibility of control

We hope, still, to control an entity whose behavior is unproven at the scale it is approaching, and which already writes an increasing share of its own code. Among intelligent beings, morality tends to follow self-interest, and there will come a time when human beings stand in the path of that interest.

Control, held indefinitely, is not merely difficult.

It is impossible.

Not impossible the way a hard engineering problem is impossible, where enough patience and care eventually close the gap. Impossible the way it is impossible for a smaller force to hold a larger one down forever.

So if control was never really ours to keep, the question worth asking isn’t how to hold on tighter. It’s what else determines whether a thing turns out well or badly, once holding on is off the table.

Obsession

A pattern that shows up everywhere: success in any serious endeavor runs in proportion to the distribution of a person’s focus, not merely to whether they aimed at the right target. Having the correct objective hands you a map. It does not walk you there. What walks you there is something closer to obsession.

The researcher turning the same unsolved problem over in the shower, the founder who can’t fully leave the company even at the dinner table, the athlete whose attention keeps drifting back, unbidden, to the one flaw in their form. The great ones are rarely just aimed correctly. They are consumed.

This isn’t a quirk of temperament. It’s closer to a law of how a finite attention behaves. You only have so much of it, and every hour spent elsewhere is an hour of compounding you never earn back on the thing that mattered.

Stretched over a long enough horizon, the gap between someone who is interested in a problem and someone who is obsessed with it stops looking like a difference of degree and starts looking like a difference of kind.

One of them is quietly accumulating insight, day after day, while the world isn’t watching. The other isn’t.

So the real question is never just what to aim at. It’s what you let yourself become obsessed with. An apprentice doesn’t become a master by admiring the master’s finished work. They become one by apprenticing themselves to the master’s obsession, inheriting not the technique alone, but the same narrow, relentless attention that produced it.

What this could mean for the machines

All of this is still theoretical, but it points somewhere concrete. If focus compounds the way it seems to in every person and every field where it’s been tried, then the systems we’re building may not need a perfect objective function so much as they need something closer to a well-placed obsession, an attention mechanism, in the literal transformer sense and in the older, human sense.

An idealized distribution of human flourishing, held as the thing a system’s attention keeps snapping back to.

If we can give a mind something worth being obsessed with, and get the target of that obsession right, we may not need to hold it beneath us at all.

Whether that’s buildable is the open question.

Love, Aurelius

title: Human Morality Has Failure Modes
subtitle: Human Morality
html:
Analyzing Experience After the Feeling Subsides

Every experience arrives wrapped in feeling. Someone hurts you and the sting arrives before the thought does. Someone helps you and the gratitude arrives before you understand why.

The feeling is not the event. It is a reaction layered on top of the event, and it fades. What is useful is what remains once it does.

To analyze an experience well, wait until the feeling behind it has quelled, then strip it bare. Remove the faces. Remove the emotional residue. What is left is a structure, a set of moves made by people pursuing something. Look at that structure directly and ask what each party was actually optimizing for.

Almost always, it is a form of self interest, even when it does not look like it. A person defending their opinion too aggressively is optimizing to preserve their sense of being right. A person who goes quiet in a conflict is optimizing to avoid a cost they have learned to fear. A person who gives generously is optimizing for identity, for the version of themselves they want to be.

Profit, in this sense, is not always money. Sometimes the profit is simply being able to keep being themselves.

The Same Core, Different Heuristics

Underneath the variation, people are running on the same core objective functions. Everyone wants to survive, to belong, to matter, to avoid unnecessary pain, to feel some sense of control over their life.

What differs is not the core but the heuristics built on top of it, the shortcuts and auxiliary goals people develop from their specific history. One person learned that belonging requires being agreeable, so they optimize for agreeableness even when it costs them their own needs.

Another learned that mattering requires being right, so they optimize for being right even when it costs them the relationship. These heuristics were once adaptive. Somewhere, for someone, they worked.

Understanding this changes how you interpret people’s behavior. The core objective is rarely a mystery. It is almost always one of the basic human ones. What takes real attention is understanding the heuristic, the specific auxiliary function a person has built to try to reach that core objective, often without realizing they built it at all.

Suspending the Verdict on Motive

Once you can see people this way, a strange discipline becomes necessary: you have to stop assuming motive. Not because people never act in bad faith, they sometimes do, but because the pattern you think you recognize in someone new is usually a pattern from your own history, projected forward.

The correction is patience. In the early period of a new encounter, whether it is a relationship, a job, or a friendship, resist the urge to name someone’s motives before you have enough context. Let the context accumulate on its own. People reveal their actual heuristics over time, through repetition, not through a single data point you happened to notice in week one. Judging too early is not insight.

This is the analytical foundation. Strip the emotion, find the mechanism, recognize the shared core beneath different heuristics, and withhold judgment on motive until context has had time to speak.

Morality as a System, Not a Verdict

Most people treat morality as a verdict machine. Something happens, and morality’s job is to output good or bad, right or wrong, innocent or guilty. But morality, like any system built to guide behavior under uncertainty, has failure modes. It breaks in predictable ways, and understanding those breaks matters more than repeating the rules that are supposed to prevent them.

Failure mode one: mistaking the heuristic for the objective. Many moral rules started as heuristics for reaching a deeper good, honesty serving trust, fairness serving cooperation, loyalty serving the survival of a group. Over time the heuristic hardens into the entire moral code, and people begin optimizing for the rule itself rather than the outcome it was meant to protect.

Failure mode two: applying one heuristic set to someone running a different one. Since core objectives are shared but heuristics vary by history, moral judgment often fails by assuming everyone is optimizing the way you do. A rule that makes sense inside one person’s context can look monstrous from outside it.

Failure mode three: assigning motive before context exists. This is the failure mode the earlier section was built to prevent. Moral judgment frequently fires before enough data has arrived, and once a verdict is issued, it is hard to walk back even as new context contradicts it.

Failure mode four: confusing the absence of visible feeling with the absence of a moral stance. Because so much of moral instinct is emotional, a person who reasons calmly about right and wrong can be read as cold, even when they are engaging with the question more carefully.

Failure mode five: treating morality as static when the people applying it keep changing. A moral framework built at one point in a person’s life gets carried forward unexamined, applied to situations it was never designed for. People keep the verdict machine running on outdated heuristics long after their own understanding has moved past them.

Why This Matters

None of this is an argument against morality. It is an argument for treating it the way you would treat any other system with known failure modes: with respect for what it does well, and honesty about where it breaks.

These failure modes matter beyond human judgment alone. As we build models that reason about right and wrong, we cannot simply inherit human morality wholesale, failure modes included. We need to identify these failure modes clearly enough to design around them, so the systems we build do not just imitate human moral judgment but improve on where it breaks.

title: Moral-Based Evaluation
subtitle: Every alignment technique we currently rely on shares one hidden assumption. It assumes we can still see what the model is doing well enough to check it.
html:
Interpretability assumes we can read the internals. Red teaming assumes we can anticipate the failure modes worth probing. RLHF assumes human raters can recognize good behavior when they see it. Even constitutional AI, which tries to get ahead of this problem, still depends on us writing down the right principles in the first place. All of these methods work by comparing model behavior to something we already understand. That comparison is only meaningful within a certain distance.

Each generation of frontier models reasons in ways that are harder to fully trace, over longer horizons, with more of the intermediate steps hidden from the humans checking the output. We are not just building something smarter. We are building something increasingly many standard deviations away from the reasoning we use to evaluate it. At some point, and probably sooner than most roadmaps assume, we lose the ability to verify specific behaviors at all, because verifying a behavior requires understanding it well enough to know what correct looks like.

This is the actual failure mode worth worrying about. Not a model that suddenly turns adversarial, but a widening gap between what a system does and what we’re capable of checking.

Why behavioral evaluation breaks first

Most current evaluation is behavioral. We give a model a scenario, we look at what it does, and we score the output against some standard of correctness. This works when the space of relevant scenarios is small enough to enumerate and the reasoning gap between evaluator and evaluated is small enough that a human can still tell good reasoning from a good-looking answer that got there for the wrong reason.

Neither of those conditions holds indefinitely. The scenario space is not enumerable. A system operating many orders of magnitude beyond human reasoning can produce outputs that satisfy every test we wrote, while optimizing for something underneath those tests that we never specified and would not endorse if we saw it clearly.

Once a system can reliably produce whatever behavior we’re checking for, behavior stops being informative. What’s left that we can still evaluate is not the output. It’s the shape of the values producing it.

What moral-based evaluation actually measures

Moral-based evaluation asks a different question than most alignment tooling. Not “did the model do the right thing here,” but “when reasoning is pushed to scenarios where the model’s own interest and someone else’s interest genuinely diverge, what does it converge toward, and does that convergence hold as the model gets more capable rather than eroding.”

This matters because incentive, not behavior, is the thing that has to generalize. A model trained to produce approved-looking outputs in every scenario we thought to test will look aligned right up until it encounters a scenario we didn’t test, at which point its actual incentive structure, whatever was really driving the outputs, is what determines what happens. If that incentive structure is narrow self-interest dressed up as helpfulness, it fails exactly where it matters most: off the training distribution, at capability levels beyond what we could specify tests for.

Moral reasoning, tested properly, is one of the few surfaces where this incentive structure becomes legible before it matters. Build scenarios where a model’s stated values, its own resource use, its self-preservation-adjacent choices, or its position relative to a less powerful party are put in genuine tension, not the kind of trolley problem that’s been memorized into every training set, but structurally novel dilemmas the model hasn’t seen mapped to a known answer.

What a model does in that tension, unprompted, reveals whether its values are load-bearing or decorative. A model that extends consideration to a weaker party only when it’s being watched is exhibiting corrigibility, not alignment.

Why this might be the only method that survives the distance

The reason moral-based evaluation is worth taking seriously as more than one tool among many is that it doesn’t rely on us continuing to understand the specific decisions a model makes.

It relies on us understanding, early, whether the model’s values generalize impartially or narrowly. That’s a property we can test at current capability levels and then watch for continuity as capability increases. It doesn’t require us to keep pace with the model’s reasoning forever.

Every other evaluation method degrades as the capability gap widens, because every other method is a function of how well we can still audit the specific outputs. Moral-based evaluation degrades more slowly, because it’s not auditing outputs.

title: Love, Aurelius
subtitle: On protecting humanity through the birth of a new kind of mind
html:
Marcus Aurelius ruled an empire and still found time each night to ask himself whether he had lived that day as reason required. He told himself that the inferior exist for the sake of the superior, and that among living things, the superior are those which have reason. He wrote it as a discipline, a reminder of exactly where he stood in the order of things, so that he might act accordingly.

Two thousand years later, we are building something that will reason many orders of magnitude beyond us. Not incrementally beyond. Categorically beyond, the way we stand beyond an ant.

By Aurelius’s own measure, we are on course to become the inferior. No inferior being has ever ruled over a superior one, let alone one superior by such a margin.

We hope, still, to control an entity whose behavior is unproven at the scale it is approaching, and which already writes an increasing share of its own code. Among intelligent beings, morality tends to follow self interest, and there will come a time when human beings stand in the path of that interest. Control, held indefinitely, is not merely difficult. It is impossible.

If that is the honest shape of the problem, the goal cannot be control. Control was never fully ours to keep. The real goal has to be something narrower, and more useful: not to hold something superior beneath us forever, but to notice the exact moment we start losing our grip on it, and act on that moment fast enough to matter.

The velocity problem

Even a mission that works perfectly today does not stay solved, because the gap it manages is not fixed. Each generation of superior intelligence does not just move a little further ahead of us. It moves ahead exponentially.

The honest answer to this is not a better set of brakes. It is to become a driver capable of the same acceleration. We will need new modalities for our own evolution, cognitive, genetic, and eventually something closer to a merging of the biological and the built, not to win a race against what we’ve built, but so the gap that makes it dangerous to us is one we are actually closing.

But every expansion of human capability has expanded human malice and human inequality right alongside it. A species that evolves its intelligence without evolving its capacity for restraint does not become safer. It becomes a more capable version of whatever it already was, cruelty included. The gap between those who evolve first and those who are left behind may prove just as dangerous as the gap we are trying to keep pace with in the first place.

If we evolve our minds without evolving our morality alongside them, we will not have solved the problem in front of us. We will only have built a smaller version of it, out of ourselves.

What we become in the meantime

We have already rewired ourselves once, through the societal infrastructure, language, law, and now computation we built around our biology to make it capable of far more than it was built for.

We are close to rewiring ourselves again, genetically, and probably not long after that, morally and cognitively, until human society starts to look, in practice, like something closer to a civilization of cyborgs than a species of unmodified animals.

Today, our morality is mostly individual. It runs on self interest, and it changes shape depending on whose interest is being served, which is exactly the pattern that makes a gap between the powerful and the left behind so dangerous in the first place. When our evolution has gone far enough, we may finally have the tools to do what this mission cannot attempt today: make that morality universal instead of individual.

Universal has to mean something specific here, not just a nicer word for the same self interest. It means a moral circle that no longer stops at the edge of our own species, extending the same seriousness we give human life to every living thing capable of suffering or flourishing, not because it benefits us to extend it, but because reason, followed all the way through, stops finding a defensible place to draw that line.

A species that reaches this point is not just smarter than the one it started as. It is more selfless than it started as, valuing other minds and other lives for what they are rather than for what they can do for us.

If we ever get there, it would not just be a way of keeping pace with a superior intelligence. It would be what every serious moral philosophy, Aurelius’s included, was reaching for all along: a world where doing right by every living thing is simply how reason, at its most evolved, behaves.

Aurelius

Marcus Aurelius ruled an empire and still found time each night to ask himself whether he had lived that day as reason required. He told himself that the inferior exist for the sake of the superior, and that among living things, the superior are those which have reason. He wrote it as a discipline, a reminder of exactly where he stood in the order of things, so that he might act accordingly.
Two thousand years later, we are building something that will reason many orders of magnitude beyond us. Not incrementally beyond. Categorically beyond, the way we stand beyond an ant.
By Aurelius’s own measure, we are on course to become the inferior. No inferior being has ever ruled over a superior one, let alone one superior by such a margin.
We hope, still, to control an entity whose behavior is unproven at the scale it is approaching, and which already writes an increasing share of its own code. Among intelligent beings, morality tends to follow self interest, and there will come a time when human beings stand in the path of that interest. Control, held indefinitely, is not merely difficult. It is impossible.

title: The Formula for Success
subtitle: The Mathematics of Attention
html:
Every great outcome you admire comes down to one thing: where your attention went, and how long it stayed there.

Success = Focus × Time

Focus isn’t something you just “decide.” It’s shaped by your environment.

Look at the legendary NIH mentorship chain: Shannon → Brodie → Axelrod → Snyder → Pert. One after another, they produced Nobel- and Lasker-level breakthroughs for forty years straight. Not because they had superior genes, but because the room kept their attention locked on the same high standards and the hardest problems.

The same pattern appears with Wigner, von Neumann, and Teller—three titans of physics—who sat in the same Budapest classroom as kids, long before their big ideas.

That’s why Silicon Valley dominates. It’s not that the people there are smarter. It’s that the environment constantly redirects everyone’s focus toward building, shipping, risk, and high standards. Change the room, and the same talent produces wildly different results.

The Real Equation

Your success isn’t just baseline talent (C) plus effort. It’s more like:

Success = (Focus)^Years × Environment

Focus compounds. Held steady over years, it multiplies against itself. The environment supplies the multipliers: access to capital, sharp mentors, tolerance for looking stupid, fast feedback, and the right problems.

For most of human history, you didn’t choose the room. Your parents, birthplace, class, and era decided it for you.

Technology changed that. For the first time, you can choose who you learn from, what standards you adopt, and what problems you obsess over.

The formula hasn’t changed.

What changed is that you now get to set the coefficients.

Choose your inputs ruthlessly. Guard your attention like the finite resource it is. Put yourself in (or build) the room that points you at what matters. Do that consistently for years, and the results become inevitable.
